identity_review.basis: The preferred working identification is that George Glasgw in Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder muster obligation was the adult George Glasgow who witnessed the 17 February 1605 baptism of George, son of James Glasgow in provisionally read Muirestoun. The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

status: Printed decree and summary page images inspected 17 October 2026; original Council register not inspected
note: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments. The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). This supports the Libberton place identification, in the same parish setting as Quothquan and near Biggar’s Lindsaylands; it does not identify a seventeenth-century occupier. This is a probable interpretation of James’s residence, not a parish supplied literally by the decree. White Castle in Garvald and Bara, East Lothian, is a real alternative place. The decree also deals with a Perthshire group; document order alone does not put every accused person in Clydesdale. No kinship is stated.

Glasgow-1376.role: James Glasgow in Whitecastle, reported imprisoned for refusing oath

Glasgow-3332.role: Possible same person only; not an additional accused person

note: Select James Glasgow-3332 as the possible working father of the 1690 apprentice James Glasgow-4131, at 46% subjective confidence. The apprentice’s father is expressly named. His uncommon full name, weaving occupation, specific Lindsayland residence and death before 1690 strongly favour identification with the weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680. Glasgow-3332 is an existing compatible account already compared with that later Biggar weaver; prefer this qualified reuse to creating another same-name father. The overall 46% applies to identifying the named documentary father with that profile, including its unresolved adult identity; it does not express doubt about the explicit father–son wording. The supporting locality and trade are one combined identity argument, not independent proofs. Glasgow-3332’s independent identity is unresolved. Its estimated 1630/1634 birth and Biggar birthplace do not independently prove the 1680 match, and its inherited John-1086 parent and 1648 Johne child attachments cannot be used circularly to establish it. The alternative 1624 Quothquan-weaver identification is retained; that much earlier decedent is a poor father-generation fit for an ordinary 1690 apprenticeship, but the apprentice has no recorded age. Whitecastle James-1376 remains a compatible possible identity of the later weaver, potentially the same man as James-3332, with no merge. The Edinburgh weaver James-1150 remains a weaker comparison: identifying him with the master active in 1693 would conflict with the father being dead in 1690, but that master’s identity is itself inferred. The 1690 apprentice may still be the 1696 apprentice James-4114 after a cancelled first indenture; the different master and the father’s death must be reconciled before merging them. The 1696 father proposal stays unchanged. No mother, spouse or vital field is transferred or altered. James-3332’s 25% father and Robert-3407’s 23% father hypothesis remain unchanged; the two proposed sons are not proved brothers. This adds one selected profile connection, not a newly discovered son, independent source, or proved pedigree.

note: Robert Glasgow-1538, Margaret Brash’s husband, is probably the older widower represented by Robert Glasgow-1530. Both accounts claim the same Barony marriage, 6 November 1803, OPR 622/70/252. The older account has a coherent local sequence: marriage to Elizabeth Jack in 1789, her death or burial in 1802, marriage to Margaret Brash in 1803, and a Glasgow weaver’s burial or death in 1839 aged 79. That age favours the Robert baptised at Wandell and Lamington on 17 February 1760, whose indexed parents are James Glasgow and Marion Saidler, over the 1755, 1758 and 1784 births. James Glasgow-1120 and Marion Sadler-2849 are therefore selected as probable working parents of Robert-1538, at 62% each. The two profiles’ identical marriage citation is one event claimed twice, not independent proof that the men are identical. Neither the child-to-adult bridge nor the linkage of the 1839 weaver to the groom has been proved. The 1758 Livingston child of Abraham Glasgow and Janet Cunnyngham, the 1755 Mid Calder child of Andrew Glasgow and Janet Young, and the 1784 Glasgow child remain compatible alternatives; burial ages may be approximate. Robert-2963 and the James Glasgow-1142/Jean Simpson family remain a weaker derivative-tree comparison, not an excluded family. Robert-1538 and Robert-1530 remain separate accounts that may represent one adult, not evidence of two sons with the same name. The local working birth is now before the 17 February 1760 baptism, explicitly a probable identity rather than an exact birthday. The captured WikiTree 13 September 1784 value is retained in the comparison and as a competing child record; no live date was changed. The 62% assessments concern the 1760 named-parent roles; James-1120’s identification with the 1738 child and his earlier ancestry remain separate inherited uncertainties. Marion is assessed from the named mother in the baptism, not inferred solely from James’s spouse. Both percentages depend on the same identity chain and are not independent probabilities. This review reuses maintained index citations and earlier contributors’ readings; no original register image was newly inspected. Alexander-2822’s 1861 marriage names Robert and Margaret, but does not identify Robert’s parents. Ralph-1537 and the other attached children are not strengthened by this selection; the 1819 Janet Gilmour groom remains unproved.

note: Current father-profile review, 20 October 2026: Prefer James Glasgow-2682, the father account defined by the Edinburgh Duffe household, as the 1696 apothecary apprentice James Glasgow-4114’s probable father at 82% subjective confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 Thomas entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 13 November 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe gives an entry age of almost fifteen. The household’s James children of 16 March 1679 and 18 April 1680 fit the 1696 entry at seventeen or sixteen. Thomas is the youngest recorded son in this family, consistent with the 1699 indenture’s youngest-son description; the later recorded child, Margaret in 1691, is a daughter. This household-specific age and sibling order gives a better father-profile fit than selecting the older craftsman solely through the repeated occupational description. The James-1150 account remains compatible as another account of this same adult, not an excluded or necessarily different biological father. The 82% assesses the complete father-profile proposition, including Thomas’s inferred apprentice-to-baptism identity and the inferred common father. These clues are related and are considered together, not multiplied as independent confirmations. Neither apprentice entry names a mother, address, father’s admission date or birth date. Another matching family remains possible. The 1679 mother’s Elizabeth/Isobell attribution is retained with its existing qualification. The 1679 and 1680 James profiles remain separate, and neither is selected as the apprentice or Jean Dobie’s husband. Isobell Duffe is not assigned as James-4114’s mother. The possible cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remains unresolved; its father was deceased, while a same-name Edinburgh master appears in 1693.
